founded.what: The year the family, rooted at Aÿ since 1522 by its own account, founded the house, which settled at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ in cellars bought in 1912.

place: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows its own vines around Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, the Clos des Goisses among them, buys more fruit and makes the wine itself.

story: The Philipponnat family has been rooted at Aÿ since 1522, by its own account, and the house dates itself from 1910. In 1912 the family bought the eighteenth century cellars and buildings of the Albert Vallet house at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ and moved its work there the next year. In 1935 the head of the house bought growers' plots on the steep slope of Les Goisses above the Marne, against the advice of fellow merchants to keep to blending, and joined them into one walled vineyard. The house holds it to be the first single vineyard Champagne. From 1946 the house kept a perpetual reserve, blending each harvest with part of the blend before it. On the death of the head of the house in 1963 his son-in-law succeeded him, and from 1980 to 1987 the owners of the Gosset house held a majority of its shares. From 1987 the house belonged to the Marie Brizard group, and on 20 November 1997 the Boizel Chanoine Champagne group bought it, by the chronology of the Union des Maisons de Champagne; that group later took the name Lanson-BCC.

style.line: Pinot Noir led, vinous and dry: part of the wine is made in oak, part without malolactic conversion, over a perpetual reserve kept since 1946.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir leads, about two thirds of Réserve Perpétuelle with a third of Chardonnay and a touch of Meunier, by the house; its own vines lie around Mareuil-sur-Aÿ and Aÿ.
style.reserve: A perpetual reserve since 1946, by the house: each new harvest is blended with part of the year before, and each cuvée is two thirds new harvest and one third reserve wine.
style.vessels: Part of the wine in wood: 39 per cent of the reserve wines for the release on the 2020 harvest and 56 per cent for the 2021, by the house.
style.malolactic: Used with care: 27 per cent of the release on the 2021 harvest was made without it, and Clos des Goisses is made without it, by the house.
style.dosage: 8 grams a litre for Réserve Perpétuelle Brut and 4.25 for Clos des Goisses, an Extra Brut, by the house.

nv.name: Réserve Perpétuelle Brut
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, formerly Royale Réserve: Pinot Noir led and built on the perpetual reserve begun in 1946.

cuvee.name: Clos des Goisses

first.what: The vintage of the year the house bought the vineyard and first bottled its wine alone.

cuvee.rhythm: Made almost every year since the 1935, by the house's own account; critics have tasted it back to the 1964 and the 1978, and the 2013, 2014 and 2015 are among its vintages.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir led, about four fifths by the house's sheets for the 2013 and the 2015, with Chardonnay for the rest.
cuvee.sites: One walled vineyard, the Clos des Goisses at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, a Premier Cru village of the Vallée de la Marne: 5.83 hectares in 14 plots by the house, facing due south above the Marne on slopes of 35 to 45 degrees.
cuvee.making: Made mainly in oak barrels, 64 per cent under wood for the 2014, with no malolactic conversion, by the house. It is an Extra Brut, 4.25 grams a litre for the 2013, 2014 and 2015 by the house's sheets, aged on its lees eight to nine years before release.
cuvee.lees: Eight years for the 2013 and nine for the 2015 before release, by the house; the L.V. releases far longer.
cuvee.young: Ripe pear and marzipan with red apple and a honeyed note that grows in the glass, in critics' notes of two vintages on release.
cuvee.aged: Biscuit, white truffle and wet stone over ripe pear, in a critic's vertical of old vintages, with toffee in another.

forms.name: Clos des Goisses Juste Rosé
forms.note: The rosé of the Clos; the 2007, 2008 and 2012 are among the vintages sold.

forms.name: Clos des Goisses L.V.
forms.note: Long vieillissement: an old vintage of the Clos released after long ageing on its lees, the 1995 and the 2000 among them.

cuvee.serve: 9 to 12 degrees Celsius, as for a fuller, oak aged Champagne, never ice cold; no need to decant; a white wine glass or a tulip.

table.house45: Philipponnat is the house of Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, in the Vallée de la Marne, founded in 1910 by a family rooted at Aÿ since 1522. Its fame rests on one vineyard, the Clos des Goisses, a steep chalk slope facing due south above the Marne. The house bought it in 1935 and bottled it on its own, the first single vineyard Champagne by its own account. The style is Pinot Noir led and vinous, with part of the wine made in oak barrels. Réserve Perpétuelle Brut is the non vintage a guest is likely to meet, and the vineyard gives its name to the prestige cuvée, Clos des Goisses.
table.house10: Philipponnat is the Pinot Noir house of Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1910, and the maker of the single vineyard Clos des Goisses.
table.cuvee45: Clos des Goisses is the wine of one walled vineyard at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, and Philipponnat's prestige cuvée. The slope faces due south above the Marne and climbs at up to forty five degrees, enclosed by a wall since 1887. It is about four fifths Pinot Noir, with Chardonnay for the rest. Most of it is made in oak barrels, and it rests eight or nine years in the cellar before release. It tastes of ripe pear, marzipan and red apple, firm and long. I serve it a touch warmer, at 9 to 12 degrees, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: Clos des Goisses is Champagne from a single vineyard, one steep chalk slope above the Marne, Pinot Noir led and made mostly in oak. May I open a bottle with your main course?
table.cuvee10: Clos des Goisses is the single vineyard Champagne of Philipponnat, Pinot Noir led, from a steep slope above the Marne at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ.
table.cuvee20: Philipponnat makes Clos des Goisses as a vintage wine from one walled vineyard facing due south above the Marne. It is about four fifths Pinot Noir and made mostly in oak, with ripe pear, marzipan and red apple.

guests.a: It comes from a local word for a very steep slope, not from a saint or a family, and the vineyard climbs at up to forty five degrees above the Marne.

guests.q: Is it a Blanc de Noirs?
guests.a: No. It is about four fifths Pinot Noir, but Chardonnay is part of the blend, so it is neither a Blanc de Noirs nor a Blanc de Blancs.

guests.q: Is Clos des Goisses a Grand Cru?
guests.a: No. Mareuil-sur-Aÿ is a Premier Cru village, so a single vineyard wine need not come from a Grand Cru village; the slope itself is what sets it apart.

guests.q: Are there other single vineyard Champagnes?
guests.a: Yes, a few. The house holds Clos des Goisses to be the first, bought in 1935; Krug's Clos du Mesnil and Billecart-Salmon's Clos Saint-Hilaire came much later.

traps: The class sheet prints Clos de Goisses; the label reads Clos des Goisses, with des, not de.
Clos des Goisses is a lieu-dit owned by Philipponnat, not an appellation.
It is not a blanc de noirs: Chardonnay is part of the blend.
Mareuil-sur-Aÿ is premier cru, so a single-vineyard wine need not come from a grand cru village.

questions.exp: Clos des Goisses is Philipponnat's, at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ. Le Clos Saint-Hilaire is Billecart-Salmon's Pinot Noir vineyard, Grande Sendrée is Drappier's of the Aube and Le Mesnil is Salon's Blanc de Blancs.

questions.q: In which year did the Boizel Chanoine Champagne group buy Philipponnat?
questions.exp: The group bought the house on 20 November 1997. 1910 is the founding, 1935 the purchase of the Clos des Goisses and 1987 the year the house joined the Marie Brizard group.

questions.exp: Clos des Goisses is about four fifths Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, made mainly in oak barrels with no malolactic conversion. It is not a Blanc de Noirs, and Chardonnay alone is the Blanc de Blancs of Salon or Delamotte.

report: Built on the library's p-philipponnat and w-clos-des-goisses, contradicting neither: founded 1910, the Clos bought in 1935 and first bottled that year, Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, partly barrel fermented, malolactic used selectively, low dosage; their traps are kept word for word.
The library names Royale Réserve as the non vintage wine; the house's pages call it Réserve Perpétuelle Brut, formerly Royale Réserve, which the record follows and the integrator should see.

First bottling: the library and Fine and Rare say the 1935 was bottled alone; Decanter alone says the name came in the 1950s with the 1951 the first sold under a Clos label, so the refuter cut that claim for want of a second source.

Walled: the house's own page says a wall has enclosed the Clos since 1887, and Decanter calls it walled; an earlier record of this tab (billecart-salmon, questions[0].exp) stopped calling it walled for want of a source, which the lead may now restore.
Size: 5.83 hectares in 14 plots by the house, 5.5 by the Union des Maisons de Champagne and some house pages; the record gives the house's figure in cuvee.sites alone.

Ownership: the Union's chronology gives the son-in-law's succession in 1963, the Gosset owners' majority 1980 to 1987, the Marie Brizard group 1987 to 1997 (also the Hachette guide) and the purchase of 20 November 1997; a holding by Marie Brizard in the 1970s is in one source only and is left out, as is the year the group became Lanson-BCC.
Nobody living is named: the founders and the head of 1935 are described, their dates not found; the son-in-law and the head of the house from 2000 are described.

The blend: 85 per cent Pinot Noir for the 2013 and 78 for the 2015 by the house, said as about four fifths or a little more; the dosage of 4.25 grams a litre is the house's for 2013, 2014 and 2015, though its general Clos page says 4.

L.V.: which vintage was the first L.V. differs between accounts (the 1995 and the 2000), so no first is given; how Juste Rosé gets its colour, and why it carries the name, rest on one account each and are left out.

The young glass is drawn from critics' notes of the 2012 (ripe pear and marzipan, reproduced by Wine.com) and the 2014 (red apple and honey, Tatler Asia); the aged glass is Decanter's vertical (a 1986 and a 1979). style.lees is empty, since no page read gives the non vintage wine's time on lees, and cuvee.bottle is empty.
kind.code: NM was not read on a label; it is inferred from the house owning vines and making the wine, and the Union lists it among its houses; a refuter should read a label.
The serving temperature is the Codex's reference for a fuller, oak aged Champagne; the house's own figure was not found.

changed: story: the son-in-law no longer ran the house from 1963 to 1987; the Union's chronology gives his succession in 1963 and the Gosset owners' majority from 1980, so the record says he succeeded in 1963 and gives no end.
story, questions[1].exp: the Marie Brizard group from 1987 to 1997 added, by the Union's chronology and the Hachette guide; 1987 in the options is now the year the house joined that group.
story, cuvee.first.what: the name of the 1950s and the 1951 as the first sold under a Clos label cut, since Decanter alone gives it.

questions[1].q: by the trade union's chronology cut from the stem, since the Union des Maisons de Champagne is a body of the houses, not a trade union, and the stem needs no source; the keys are not frozen.
cuvee.rhythm: made almost every year since 1935 by the house's own account, and the vintages named without saying what the house shows today.
cuvee.blend: the four fifths given as the house's for the 2013 (85 per cent) and the 2015 (78).
cuvee.forms[0]: named for its pale colour cut (one account); the 2015 rosé, not found, replaced by the 2012 (Berry Bros. and Rudd, Justerinis).
table.cuvee45: sun from sunrise to sunset, a claim no source read carries, replaced by the wall of 1887 (the house); the serving temperature now 9 to 12 degrees, as cuvee.serve says.
open: NM was not read on a label: no label code was found; the Union lists the house among its members and it buys fruit beyond its vines.
The 1912 purchase of the Vallet cellars rests on the author's reading; this refuter's search of the house's own domain did not return it.
The Clos's size is 5.83 hectares by the house and 5.5 by the Union and Decanter; the record keeps the house's figure.
